## What the model says

Signal detection theory (Green & Swets, 1966) says that each trial yields a value of evidence on one axis
and that the observer answers "old" (or "signal") when the evidence exceeds a criterion $k$. Noise trials
(new items) draw the evidence from a distribution located at 0 with scale 1; for the normal distribution the
scale is the SD. Signal trials (old items) draw it from the same distribution, moved to $\delta$ and stretched
by a factor $s$. The false-alarm rate FA is the probability of "old" on a noise trial, the area under the noise
density to the right of $k$, and the hit rate H the same area under the signal density. With $F$ the
cumulative distribution function of the standard distribution (location 0, scale 1) that `dist` names,

$$
\text{FA} = P(\text{"old"} \mid \text{noise}) = 1 - F(k), \qquad
\text{H} = P(\text{"old"} \mid \text{signal}) = 1 - F\!\left(\frac{k - \delta}{s}\right).
$$

bmm calls $k$ `criterion` and $s$ `sdratio`. Its sensitivity parameter `d`, the slider on this page, sets the
distance $\delta$ between the two locations: $\delta = d\,\sqrt{(1 + s^2)/2}$, so `d` is the distance divided
by the root-mean-square of the two scales. With equal scales ($s = 1$) `d` and $\delta$ are the same, and `d` is
the familiar $d'$; with unequal scales `d` is the index called $d_a$, and $\delta$ is larger than `d` when $s > 1$.
`bias` places the same boundary $k$ but measures it from the midpoint between the two locations: `bias`
$= k - \delta/2$. Under equal variance it is the index usually written $c$; 0 is the midpoint, and positive values
put the boundary closer to the signal, so the observer answers "new" more often. A row of data holds the number
of "old" responses out of `n_trials` noise or signal trials, which is binomial with probability FA or H.

`dist` sets the shape of both densities: `normal`, `logistic`, `gumbel_min` or `gumbel_max`. The logistic is
symmetric like the normal, with heavier tails. The two Gumbel (extreme-value) distributions are skewed, mirror
images of each other, and their location 0 is the peak, not the mean. Each enters with scale 1, so under
logistic and Gumbel noise `d` and `criterion` are in units of that scale, not of the SD (the standard logistic
has SD $\pi/\sqrt{3} \approx 1.81$, the standard Gumbel $\pi/\sqrt{6} \approx 1.28$).

## The task

One trial presents one item: a studied or a new word in recognition, a display with or without the target in
detection. The participant answers old or new, yes or no. bmm fits counts: each row of the data holds `n_old`,
the number of "old" responses, out of `n_trials` trials, with `stimulus` coded 0 for noise and 1 for signal. No
task setting enters the likelihood, so the Task settings panel stays empty. How many trials a row has decides
the spread of its counts, not the probability of an "old" response.

## Explore

The top panel draws both evidence densities and the criterion; drag the line or move the slider. The shaded
area under the noise density to the right of the line is the false-alarm rate, the shaded area under the signal
density the hit rate, and the bars repeat the two numbers. With `criterion` selected, raising `d` moves the
signal density to the right and raises the hit rate alone, and moving the criterion changes both rates
together. `sdratio` above 1 widens the signal density, so the hit rate changes more slowly as the criterion
moves through it. Switching to `bias` keeps the boundary where it is and gives its position from the midpoint
between the two locations, which then appears as a dotted line; with `bias` held fixed, a change in `d` drags
the criterion along with the midpoint.

The ROC (receiver operating characteristic) panel plots the hit rate against the false-alarm rate for every
position of the criterion, at the current `d` and `sdratio`; the circle is the current criterion and the grey
diagonal is chance, where hits and false alarms are equally likely. With equal scales the normal and logistic
ROCs are symmetric about the other diagonal, from the top left to the bottom right. The Gumbel ROCs are not, even
at `sdratio` = 1: under `gumbel_min` the point farthest from the chance line moves to low false-alarm rates, as
it does under normal noise with `sdratio` above 1, and under `gumbel_max` to high ones.

The sliders span bmm's default priors, the prior mean ± 3 SD, written normal(mean, SD): `d` normal(1, 1), from
−2 to 4; `criterion` normal(0.5, 1.5), from −4 to 5; `bias` normal(0, 1.5), from −4.5 to 4.5. bmm estimates
`sdratio` on the log scale with a normal(0, 0.3) prior, so its slider moves in steps of log(`sdratio`), from a
ratio of $e^{-0.9} = 0.41$ to $e^{0.9} = 2.46$, and the box shows the ratio. Unless a model formula names
`sdratio`, bmm fixes it at 1. The dashed bars and the dashed ROC are the prior means, `d` = 1, `criterion` =
0.5 (the same boundary as `bias` = 0 at these values) and `sdratio` = 1, so at the start values they lie under
the solid ones.

## Across task settings

The yes/no model has no task setting in its likelihood, so there is no design variable to vary while the
parameters stay fixed. What an experiment can vary between conditions is where the observer puts the criterion,
and that is what identifies `sdratio`. One condition gives one pair of rates, one point on the ROC, and a point
does not fix the curve. `sdt_d()`, bmm's function for the equal-variance `d` of a hit and a false-alarm rate,
gives an observer with `sdratio` = 1, the same criterion and another `d` who produces the same two rates. Once
`sdratio` differs from 1, that observer's ROC appears as the dotted curve, through the circle. Two rates cannot
fix three parameters (`d`, `criterion`, `sdratio`), so `sdratio` needs conditions that share `d` and move the
boundary. In bmm's formula syntax, `d ~ 1` keeps one `d` for all conditions and `criterion ~ 0 + condition`
gives each condition its own criterion: that is the design for a base-rate or payoff manipulation. A criterion
that is the same in every row lets `sdratio` trade against `d`, and `bmm()` warns for it. With `bias` in the
formula instead, a constant `bias` moves the criterion whenever `d` changes, so conditions that differ in `d`
also give several points on the curve; the estimate then rests on the assumption that the observer keeps the
bias, not the criterion, constant. <span id="sdtyn-across-now"></span>

The code updates with the controls. `sdt_yn()` names the data columns (`response`, the count of "old"
responses; `stimulus`; `n_trials`) and the evidence distribution,
`dsdt_yn()` returns the log likelihood of the counts of "old" responses, and `bmm()` estimates the parameters
from data; `my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs Stan through brms. `dsdt_yn()` takes `sdratio`
as the ratio itself, while the model estimates its log. See the
[signal detection article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_sdt.html) and the reference pages for
[`sdt_yn()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdt_yn.html),
[`dsdt_yn()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdt_yn_dist.html) and
[`sdt_d()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/SDTdist.html).
